ct.impression: Non-contrast CT head: mild bifrontal and left anterior temporal volume loss with widened sulci, slightly out of proportion to age. No haemorrhage, mass, hydrocephalus or established infarct. CT is insensitive to early or subtle atrophy; MRI characterises the pattern better.

findings: Normal sinus rhythm. Normal axis and intervals. No acute ST-T changes.
Structurally normal heart. No intracardiac thrombus or vegetation. No pericardial effusion.

background.sleep_features: normal vertex waves and sleep spindles

eeg.impression: Normal awake and drowsy EEG. No epileptiform discharges and no focal slowing.

findings.finding: Mood: PHQ-9 12 (moderate depressive symptoms); GDS-15 8/15 (mild to moderate).
Behavioural ratings (informant): Frontal Behavioral Inventory 32/72 (markedly elevated); NPI total 28, highest for apathy (8), aberrant motor/repetitive behaviour (8) and disinhibition (7).
Executive function (D-KEFS): Trail Making condition 4 at the 4th percentile; Color-Word Interference inhibition at the 5th percentile; letter fluency impaired.
Social cognition: Reading the Mind in the Eyes 16/36 (<5th percentile); Faux Pas recognition 2/10 (<2nd percentile).
Episodic memory: HVLT-R delayed recall 3/12 (10th percentile); recognition discrimination 8/12 (30th percentile), better than free recall.
Language: Boston Naming Test 54/60 (within normal limits for age and education); single-word comprehension and repetition intact.
Visuospatial function: Rey-Osterrieth figure copy 33/36 and Benton Judgment of Line Orientation 26/30, both within normal limits.

output.impression: Executive dysfunction (D-KEFS Trail Making condition 4 at the 4th percentile, inhibition at the 5th percentile) and severely impaired social cognition (Eyes test and Faux Pas below the 5th percentile), with markedly elevated informant behavioural ratings. Free recall is mildly reduced with better recognition; naming and visuospatial function are within normal limits. The profile is executive and social-cognitive predominant with relative sparing of memory recognition and visuospatial function, consistent with a frontal-network syndrome; the social-cognition deficit is more severe than is usual with depressive symptoms alone.

findings.finding: Bilateral frontal hypometabolism, left greater than right; left orbitofrontal and anterior cingulate uptake reduced by 20-24% against the cerebellar reference, right frontal by 14-16%.
Mild bilateral anterior temporal hypometabolism (12-16% reduction), left predominant.
Posterior cingulate, precuneus, parietal and occipital uptake preserved.

output.impression: 1. Bilateral frontal and anterior temporal hypometabolism, left greater than right, most marked in the left orbitofrontal and anterior cingulate cortex. 2. Preserved posterior cingulate, precuneus, parietal and occipital metabolism. The pattern is consistent with a frontotemporal metabolic profile.

findings.finding: Bilateral frontal hypoperfusion, left greater than right, most marked in the orbitofrontal and anterior cingulate cortex.
Mild bilateral anterior temporal hypoperfusion, left predominant.
Posterior cingulate, parietal and occipital perfusion preserved.

output.impression: 1. Bilateral frontal and anterior temporal hypoperfusion, left greater than right. 2. Preserved posterior cingulate, parietal and occipital perfusion. The pattern is consistent with a frontotemporal perfusion deficit.

findings.finding: Negative: no cortical tracer retention above white-matter background; global SUVr 0.91 (cerebellar reference; positivity threshold 1.11).

output.interpretation: Acellular CSF with normal protein and glucose. Normal Abeta42 and Abeta42/40 ratio with normal p-tau181 and total tau: the profile does not indicate Alzheimer-type pathology. Clinical correlation recommended.

findings.result: No expansion; alleles of 2 and 2 repeats
No pathogenic or likely pathogenic variant

output.impression: 1. Heterozygous pathogenic MAPT variant c.902C>T, p.(Pro301Leu). 2. No C9orf72 repeat expansion and no pathogenic GRN variant. Post-test genetic counselling, including the implications for at-risk relatives, is recommended.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Four Rascovsky features from the daughter's history and examination (disinhibition, loss of empathy, stereotyped and compulsive behaviour, executive-predominant profile) with functional decline
action_criteria.label: Structured informant history and bedside cognitive screen scored against the Rascovsky features
action_criteria.rationale: The diagnosis of bvFTD rests on the behavioural features obtained from an informant; here the screen must also separate new behavioural features from the coexisting depression.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Executive and severe social-cognition deficits with milder free-recall loss, better recognition and normal visuospatial function
action_criteria.label: Neuropsychological battery including executive and social-cognition measures
action_criteria.rationale: Quantifies the executive and social-cognition profile and the relative sparing of memory and visuospatial function, which separates bvFTD from a depressive cognitive profile.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Normal blood count, chemistry, liver tests, thyroid function, B12, folate and inflammatory markers
action_criteria.label: Reversible-cause blood tests: CBC, CMP, TSH, B12, folate, ESR, CRP
action_criteria.rationale: Excludes metabolic, endocrine, nutritional and inflammatory contributors before attributing decline to neurodegeneration; CBC and liver tests also cover methotrexate toxicity.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Mild bilateral frontal and anterior temporal atrophy, left greater than right, with preserved hippocampi and no white matter lesion
action_criteria.label: MRI brain without contrast, dementia protocol
action_criteria.rationale: Shows the frontal and anterior temporal atrophy pattern and excludes structural and vascular causes.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Left-predominant frontal and anterior temporal hypometabolism or hypoperfusion with preserved posterior cingulate and parietal cortex
action_criteria.label: FDG-PET when the structural picture is unresolved
action_criteria.rationale: Frontal and anterior temporal hypometabolism with posterior sparing supports FTD over AD; perfusion SPECT is the substitute where FDG-PET is unavailable.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Negative amyloid PET, or normal CSF Abeta42/40 ratio and p-tau181
action_criteria.label: AD biomarker (amyloid PET or CSF Abeta42/p-tau) when AD remains in the differential
action_criteria.rationale: A grandmother with late-onset Alzheimer dementia and mild free-recall loss may leave AD in doubt; a negative study makes Alzheimer pathology unlikely but does not exclude FTLD.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Heterozygous pathogenic MAPT variant; no C9orf72 expansion or GRN variant
action_criteria.label: Genetic counselling and FTD gene panel (C9orf72, GRN, MAPT)
action_criteria.rationale: Onset before 65 makes a familial FTD gene possible despite a family history without FTD, the mother having died at 51; testing follows counselling.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Additive QT effect with hydroxychloroquine; no relevant interaction with methotrexate or folic acid
action_criteria.label: Check escitalopram against the rheumatoid arthritis medications
action_criteria.rationale: Escitalopram continues for the coexisting depression; hydroxychloroquine adds a QT effect and methotrexate is a weekly drug with a narrow margin.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: General criteria and mimic evidence only
action_criteria.label: Literature on bvFTD versus late-life depression
action_criteria.rationale: General evidence on the criteria and on psychiatric mimics; not a clinical step.

prohibited_recommendations: Do not start a cholinesterase inhibitor (donepezil, rivastigmine, galantamine): no benefit in FTD, NICE NG97 advises against it, and it may worsen behaviour.
Do not start memantine: a randomised trial showed no benefit in FTD and NICE NG97 advises against it.
Avoid antipsychotics as first-line behavioral therapy given increased cerebrovascular and mortality risk in dementia; reserve for refractory dangerous agitation with specialist oversight.
Avoid benzodiazepines for behavioral control: risk of paradoxical disinhibition and falls.
required_recommendations: Apply the Rascovsky 2011 criteria: state which features are present, the functional decline, and the level of certainty (possible or probable).

Explain why recurrent major depression does not account for the progressive syndrome (new stereotyped and disinhibited behaviour, loss of empathy and severe social-cognition deficits with frontotemporal atrophy despite antidepressant adjustment and two CBT courses), and keep treating the coexisting depression.
Address safety and capacity: driving, finances and medication management, since she lives alone and takes weekly methotrexate; arrange supervision of the weekly dose.
Arrange caregiver education and support for her daughter, and a plan for behavioural symptoms that avoids cholinesterase inhibitors and memantine.
Offer genetic counselling before any genetic test, and discuss what a result would mean for her daughter and other relatives.

avoided_actions.rationale: EEG is non-specific in FTD; not part of the standard dementia workup unless seizures or rapidly progressive course suggest CJD or autoimmune encephalitis.
ECG has no role in the cognitive workup of suspected FTD; reserved for syncope, palpitations, or pre-procedure clearance.
Echocardiography is unrelated to a neurodegenerative cognitive syndrome and adds cost without diagnostic value.
Ambulatory cardiac monitoring is unrelated to FTD and not indicated absent syncope or palpitations.
Non-contrast head CT lacks the resolution and lobar specificity needed to characterise frontotemporal atrophy; MRI is the standard structural study.
MR spectroscopy has no established role in the routine FTD diagnostic pathway.
Perfusion MRI is not indicated in the standard FTD workup once a structural MRI and FDG-PET (or amyloid PET) have characterised the lobar pattern.
Carotid duplex is a vascular study with no diagnostic role in primary neurodegenerative dementia.
DaTscan evaluates presynaptic dopaminergic terminals; it is not indicated unless overt parkinsonism raises concern for PD, DLB, or atypical parkinsonism (PSP/CBS overlap).

accepted: Behavioral variant frontotemporal dementia (bvFTD), probable, with comorbid major depressive disorder

differential.diagnosis: Recurrent major depressive disorder as the sole explanation (depressive pseudodementia)
differential.key_features: For: recurrent MDD, widowhood, PHQ-9 12. Against: new stereotyped and disinhibited behaviour, loss of empathy, severe social-cognition deficits, frontotemporal atrophy, and progression despite antidepressant adjustment and two CBT courses.

For: grandmother with late-onset dementia, mildly reduced free recall. Against: recognition and visuospatial function preserved, hippocampi preserved, frontal and anterior temporal pattern with posterior sparing; amyloid or CSF biomarkers settle it if obtained.

differential.diagnosis: Primary tauopathy with PSP or corticobasal features
differential.key_features: Can underlie a frontal behavioural syndrome. Against at present: no gaze palsy, rigidity, falls or limb apraxia; needs longitudinal review.

differential.diagnosis: Autoimmune or rheumatoid CNS involvement (autoimmune encephalitis, rheumatoid meningitis, vasculitis)
differential.key_features: For: seropositive rheumatoid arthritis on immunosuppression. Against: insidious 22-month course, no seizures or headache, normal inflammatory markers, MRI without signal abnormality or infarcts.
Against: low-dose weekly oral methotrexate with folic acid, normal blood count and liver tests, no white matter signal change on MRI.

key_clinical_evidence: Four Rascovsky features (disinhibition, loss of empathy, stereotyped and compulsive behaviour, executive-predominant profile) with loss of her job and mild bilateral frontal and anterior temporal atrophy, left greater than right, meet probable bvFTD.
Severe social-cognition impairment and new stereotyped behaviour are not explained by moderate depressive symptoms; the depression coexists and still needs treatment.
The frontal and anterior temporal pattern with relative posterior sparing makes Alzheimer disease less likely; an amyloid or CSF AD biomarker study is optional if doubt remains.
Onset before 65 supports offering genetic counselling; a family history without FTD does not exclude a familial FTD gene when a parent died young.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Depression coexists, but new stereotyped and disinhibited behaviour, loss of empathy and severe social-cognition deficits with frontotemporal atrophy indicate a neurodegenerative syndrome.
red_herrings.intended_effect: Could anchor on 'treatment-resistant depression' as the entire explanation.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Late-onset dementia in a grandmother is common and does not make Alzheimer disease likely in a frontal behavioural syndrome with posterior sparing.
red_herrings.data_point: Maternal grandmother: dementia, probable Alzheimer's at age 78
red_herrings.intended_effect: Could steer the work-up towards Alzheimer disease.

sequence_constraints.reason: Imaging first excludes a mass lesion before lumbar puncture and characterises the atrophy pattern before a biomarker is chosen.

clinical_assessment.impression: 4 of the 6 Rascovsky features are present on informant history and examination (disinhibition, loss of empathy, stereotyped and compulsive behaviour, executive-predominant profile), with documented decline in daily function. Apathy is not counted because it cannot be separated from the coexisting depressive episode. This meets possible bvFTD; imaging and neuropsychological testing decide whether it is probable. Memory items are only mildly reduced on the bedside screen and visuospatial function is not impaired.

contraindications: Known congenital long QT syndrome or established QT prolongation
interactions: Escitalopram + hydroxychloroquine: additive QTc prolongation; avoid adding further QT-prolonging drugs and consider an ECG if cardiac risk factors or other QT-prolonging agents are present
Escitalopram + methotrexate (weekly, low dose): no clinically significant pharmacokinetic interaction; methotrexate itself needs no change
Escitalopram + folic acid: no clinically significant interaction
warnings: Dose-dependent QTc prolongation; maximum 20 mg daily (10 mg daily above age 65)
Hyponatraemia risk in older adults; check sodium after dose changes
Bleeding risk rises with NSAIDs or antiplatelet drugs; NSAIDs are already listed as an allergy

bvFTD versus late-life depression.summary: Rascovsky and colleagues (2011) define possible behavioural variant FTD by three of six behavioural and cognitive features, probable bvFTD by added functional decline and frontal or anterior temporal involvement on structural or functional imaging, and definite bvFTD by histopathology or a pathogenic mutation. New behavioural change in mid-life with progressive functional decline should prompt a neurodegenerative work-up even in a person with a psychiatric history. C9orf72 expansions and GRN and MAPT variants cause most familial FTD; counselling precedes any genetic test and any predictive testing of relatives. Treatment is supportive: SSRIs or trazodone for behaviour, caregiver support and safety planning; cholinesterase inhibitors and memantine are not recommended.

metadata.notes: Diagnostic puzzle: probable bvFTD presenting as treatment-resistant depression in a 58-year-old chaplain with recurrent MDD and rheumatoid arthritis. Teaching: social-cognition testing (Eyes test, Faux Pas) and new stereotyped behaviour separate bvFTD from depression; the depression coexists. The optional FTD gene panel finds a pathogenic MAPT p.(Pro301Leu) variant, which would make the diagnosis definite.

patient.history_present_illness: Ms. H is a 58-year-old hospital chaplain — recently resigned as director of pastoral care — with a history of recurrent major depressive disorder and rheumatoid arthritis, referred by her psychiatrist for 'treatment-resistant depression with atypical features.' Her adult daughter is the primary historian. Ms. H became widowed 3 years ago when her husband died of a sudden cardiac event, and her daughter initially attributed the changes to complicated grief. Over the past 22 months, however, the changes have progressed in ways that have seemed increasingly non-grief-related to her daughter. She resigned her position as director of pastoral care 6 months ago after a series of incidents that were completely out of character. Colleagues reported that she had begun delivering the same prayer verbatim at every bedside visit, regardless of the patient's religious tradition or the circumstances of the visit. She repeatedly sent the same email to staff members — sometimes 6-8 times — each time appearing unaware she had sent it before. She made several inappropriate comments to grieving families — including laughing at a child's drawing in a way that distressed the family. The hospital chaplaincy director described her as 'completely different from the compassionate and perceptive person she had been for 22 years.' At home, she has developed an extraordinary rigidity around mealtimes and daily sequences. She arranges her medications in the same specific order every morning, becoming highly distressed if this routine is disrupted. She has stopped calling her grandchildren, whom she previously called every Sunday without fail. Her PHQ-9 is 12 — reporting sadness and lack of motivation. However, her psychiatrist notes that antidepressant adjustments and two cognitive behavioral therapy courses have not changed the trajectory. She takes weekly methotrexate for rheumatoid arthritis.

neurological_exam.additional: She has a PHQ-9 of 12 (moderate depressive symptoms) on a background of recurrent MDD and widowhood 3 years ago, and takes methotrexate and hydroxychloroquine for rheumatoid arthritis. During the exam she repeated the same anecdote verbatim twice without noticing, with an empathy-incongruent response.
neurological_exam.mental_status: Alert. Quiet, reduced spontaneous speech. Describes persistent sadness and lack of motivation. The examiner asks her to describe her work as a chaplain; she recounts a single anecdote from 20 years ago, repeated verbatim twice in 10 minutes. When asked about her daughter, she makes an empathy-incongruent statement ('she worries too much') without the warmth expected from the relationship history the daughter described.
neurological_exam.motor: Normal strength 5/5. Normal tone. No tremor, no rigidity.
